Whirlwind
WHIRL-wind
noun
From whirl (Middle English whirlen, of Norse origin, to turn rapidly) and wind; the Hebrew ce'arah and suphah alike name the tempest that turns and sweeps, the storm-wind of God’s coming.

Biblical Definition

A whirlwind is a turning tempest — the storm-wind that sweeps up and carries off whatever it finds. In Scripture it is God’s chariot, God’s pulpit, and God’s harvest-sickle. It is His chariot when Elijah is taken: “there appeared a chariot of fire, and horses of fire, and parted them both asunder; and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven” (2Ki 2:11) — the LORD had told Elisha beforehand that He would take up His prophet so (2Ki 2:1). It is His pulpit when Job’s long argument is answered: the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind, and the answer was not an explanation but a catechism about wild goats and cloud and snow, until the man who had demanded a hearing laid his hand upon his mouth. God speaks from the storm, not around it. And it is His sickle in the prophets: “For they have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind” (Hos 8:7) — the classic statement that sin’s harvest exceeds its seed, that a nation which plants emptiness reaps ruin, and that the yield of idolatry has no stalk and no meal. Nahum sets the whole doctrine in one verse: “The LORD is slow to anger, and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked: the LORD hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet” (Nah 1:3). The tempest that terrifies the wicked is only the dust kicked up by the walking of God.

Webster 1828 Definition

A violent turning wind; a tempest that whirls and sweeps — in Scripture the chariot, the pulpit, and the judgment of God.

WHIRLWIND, a violent wind moving in a circle or spiral; a tempest that sweeps and carries off.

From whirl, to turn rapidly, and wind; Hebrew ce'arah, suphah, the storm-wind.

Elijah was carried up by a whirlwind into heaven (2Ki 2:11).

The LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind (Job 38:1) — He speaks from the storm.

They sow the wind and reap the whirlwind: sin’s harvest exceeds its seed (Hos 8:7).

Key Scripture

2Ki 2:11 — "And it came to pass, as they still went on, and talked, that, behold, there appeared a chariot of fire, and horses of fire, and parted them both asunder; and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven."

2Ki 2:1 — "And it came to pass, when the LORD would take up Elijah into heaven by a whirlwind, that Elijah went with Elisha from Gilgal."

Hos 8:7 — "For they have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind: it hath no stalk: the bud shall yield no meal: if so be it yield, the strangers shall swallow it up."

Nah 1:3 — "The LORD is slow to anger, and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked: the LORD hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet."

Modern Corruption

A storm-word flattened into a figure of speech, and a Book of Job read as a poem about the problem of pain rather than a theophany.

expand to see more

The word has thinned in modern mouths to a metaphor for a busy week, and the doctrine has thinned with it. Behind the flattening lies a settled unwillingness to grant that God governs storms — that Nahum meant what he said when he put the LORD’s way in the whirlwind and made the thunderheads the dust of His feet. So the whirlwind of Job 38 is treated as a literary device, and the book is preached as an inquiry into the problem of suffering that ends, disappointingly, without an answer. But Job did not receive an argument because he did not need one; he needed God, and God came — personally, audibly, out of the tempest — and asked him where he was when the foundations were laid. The book ends with a man silenced and satisfied. That is the answer, and only a generation that thinks God owes it explanations could miss it.

The second flattening is Hosea 8:7 reduced to a proverb about consequences. It is more than that: it is covenant judgment. Israel had sown the wind — calf-worship at Bethel, treaties with Assyria, kings set up without the LORD — and the whirlwind that came was not an impersonal blowback but the hand of a God who will not at all acquit the wicked. The harvest law stands for nations still, and for men: whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap (Gal 6:7), and the reaping is always larger than the sowing. Yet the same whirlwind that carries away the chaff carried Elijah home. To the wicked the storm is judgment; to the LORD’s servant it is a chariot. The difference is not in the weather but in whose you are.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

A turning tempest — in Scripture the chariot, the pulpit, and the judgment-harvest of God.

expand to see more

Whirlwind — whirl (to turn rapidly) + wind; Hebrew ce'arah, suphah.

It is God’s chariot: Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven (2Ki 2:11).

It is God’s pulpit: the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind (Job 38:1).

It is God’s sickle: they sow the wind and reap the whirlwind (Hos 8:7).

Nah 1:3 — the clouds are the dust of His feet; the storm is His walking.

Usage

"Elijah went up by a whirlwind: to the servant of God the storm is a chariot."

"They have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind — the harvest exceeds the seed."

"The LORD hath His way in the whirlwind: He is never merely in the calm."
